¶
'''boatswain''' (bōt′swān; colloq. and in naut. use, bō′sn), ''n.'' [Also colloq. and naut. ''boson'' (formerly in good literary use); early mod. E. ''boatswain'', ''boatson'', ''boteswayne'', < late ME. ''botswayne''; < ''boat'' + ''swain'', in the sense of ‘boy servant.’ The alleged AS. *''bātswān'' is not authorized.] '''1.''' A subordinate officer of a ship, who has charge of the rigging, anchors, cables, and cordage. {{smaller|It is his duty also to summon the crew for any evolution, and to assist the executive officer in the necessary business of the ship. His station is always on the forecastle, and a silver call or whistle is the badge of his office.}} '''2.''' A jäger or skua; any bird of the genus ''Lestris'' or ''Stercorarius''.
{{smaller block|Dr. Bessels killed three fork-tailed gulls, and two ''boatswains.''
{{right|''C. F. Hall'', Polar Expedition, p. 388.}}}}
'''3.''' A name of birds of the genus ''Phaëthon.'' See ''tropic-bird.''—{{smaller|'''Boatswain’s mate,''' an assistant of a boatswain. Boatswain’s mates inflicted corporal punishment before it was abolished.}}

'''boat-tailed''' (bōt′tāld), ''a.'' Having the tail boat-shaped. See ''boat-shaped.''

'''boattails''' (bōt′tālz), ''n. pl.'' In ''ornith.'', a name sometimes given to the American grackles, subfamily ''Quiscalinæ'', family ''Icteridæ'', from the fact that their tails are boat-shaped. See cut under ''boat-shaped.''

'''boatwright''' (bōt′rīt), ''n.'' A boat-builder.

'''bob'''<sup>1</sup> (bob), ''n.'' [Under the form ''bob'' are included several words of obscure origin, mostly colloquial and without a definite literary history, and in consequence now more or less confused in sense as well as in form. The different senses, in their noun and verb uses, have reacted on each other, and cannot now be en-

get into a puzzle.] A louse; any small insect. ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]

¶
'''bobac, bobak''' (bob′ak), ''n.'' [Pol. ''bobak.''] The Polish marmot, ''Arctomys bobac.''

'''Bobadil''' (bob′ạ-dil), ''n.'' [The name of a boastful character in Ben Jonson’s “Every Man in his Humour.”] A blustering braggart.

'''Bobadilian''' (bob-a-dil′ian), ''a.'' Pertaining to or resembling a Bobadil, or a blustering fellow who makes pretenses to prowess.

'''Bobadilism''' (bob′ạ-dil-izm), ''n.'' [< ''Bobadil'' + ''-ism.''] Blustering conduct or braggadocio.

'''bobak,''' ''n.'' See ''bobac.''

'''bobance†,''' ''n.'' [ME., also ''bobaunce,'' < OF. ''bobance'' (F. ''bombance'') = Pr. ''bobansa,'' ostentation, display, = It. ''bombanza,'' exultation. Cf. ML. ''bombicus,'' proud, ostentatious, < L. ''bombus,'' a buzzing sound: see ''bomb''<sup>2</sup>.] Boasting. ''Chaucer.''

'''bobber<sup>1</sup>''' (bob′ėr), ''n.'' [< ''bob''<sup>1</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' One who or that which bobs.—'''2.''' One who fishes with a bob.—'''3.''' One of the artificial flies of an angler’s cast.

'''bobber<sup>2</sup>†,''' ''n.'' [< ''bob''<sup>3</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' One who scoffs.
{{smaller block|Bitter taunters, dry ''bobbers,'' nyppinge gybers, and skorneful mockers of others.
{{right|''Touchstone of Complexions'' (1575).}}}}
'''2.''' A deceiver.

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|boat-shaped|606|bobbin}}</noinclude>{{nop}}'''boat-shaped''' (bōt′shāpt), ''a.'' Having the shape of a boat; navicular; cymbiform; hollow like a boat, as (in ''bot.'') the valves of some pericarps. {{smaller|Specifically, in ''ornith.'', applied to the tail of certain birds,}}
{{smaller|as the boat-tailed grackle, ''Quiscalus major'', in which the plane of the feathers of each half meets that of the other half obliquely, slanting downward and toward the median line, and thus induces a reëntrance or hollow of the upper surface and a salience or keel below.}}

[[File:century v01 p0632 c1f1.png|center|298px]]
{{c|{{smaller|Boat-shaped.—Tail of a Grackle.}}}}

'''boat-shell''' (bōt′shel), ''n.'' The English name of the shells of the genus ''Cymbium'' or ''Cymba'', belonging to the family ''Volutidæ''. See cut under ''Cymbium''.

'''boat-skid''' (bōt′skid), ''n.'' ''Naut.'', a piece of wood fastened to a ship’s side to prevent chafing when a boat is hoisted or lowered.

'''boatsman†''' (bōts′man), ''n.''   [< ''boat’s'', poss. of ''boat'', + ''man''; = D. ''bootsman'' = Sw. ''båtsman'' = Dan. ''baadsman'', boatswain.]   '''1.''' A boatswain. —'''2.''' A boatman.

'''boat-song''' (bōt′sông), ''n.'' A vocal, or occasionally an instrumental, musical composition, either intended actually to be sung while rowing or sailing or written in imitation of a song thus used. See ''barcarole''.

'''boatswain''' (bōt′swān; colloq. and in naut. use, bō′sn), ''n.''   [Also colloq. and naut. ''boson'' (formerly in good literary use); early mod. E. ''boatswain'', ''boatson'', ''boteswayne'', < late ME. ''botswayne''; < ''boat'' + ''swain'', in the sense of ‘boy servant.’ The alleged AS. *''bātswān'' is not authorized.]   '''1.''' A subordinate officer of a ship, who has charge of the rigging, anchors, cables, and cordage. {{smaller|It is his duty also to summon the crew for any evolution, and to assist the executive officer in the necessary business of the ship. His station is always on the forecastle, and a silver call or whistle is the badge of his office.}} '''2.''' A jäger or skua; any bird of the genus ''Lestris'' or ''Stercorarius''.
{{smaller block|Dr. Bessels killed three fork-tailed gulls, and two ''boatswains.''
{{right|''C. F. Hall'', Polar Expedition, p. 388.}}}}
'''3.''' A name of birds of the genus ''Phaëthon.'' See ''tropic-bird.''—{{smaller|'''Boatswain’s mate,''' an assistant of a boatswain. Boatswain’s mates inflicted corporal punishment before it was abolished.}}

'''boat-tailed''' (bōt′tāld), ''a.'' Having the tail boat-shaped. See ''boat-shaped.''

'''boattails''' (bōt′tālz), ''n. pl.'' In ''ornith.'', a name sometimes given to the American grackles, subfamily ''Quiscalinæ'', family ''Icteridæ'', from the fact that their tails are boat-shaped. See cut under ''boat-shaped.''

'''boatwright''' (bōt′rīt), ''n.'' A boat-builder.

'''bob'''<sup>1</sup> (bob), ''n.''   [Under the form ''bob'' are included several words of obscure origin, mostly colloquial and without a definite literary history, and in consequence now more or less confused in sense as well as in form. The different senses, in their noun and verb uses, have reacted on each other, and cannot now be entirely disentangled. ''Bob''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'', a cluster, etc., = Sc. ''bob'', ''bab'', a cluster, bunch, nosegay, < ME. ''bob'', ''bobbe'', a cluster; cf. Icel. ''bobbi'', a knot (''nodus'', Haldorsen), and Gael. ''babag'', a cluster, ''baban'', a tassel, fringe. In senses 5, 6, 7, rather from ''bob''<sup>1</sup>, ''v. t.'', 1; in senses 10, 11, 13, ''bob'' is short for ''bob-wig'', ''bob-stick'', ''bob-sled'', q. v.]   '''1.''' A bunch; a cluster; a nosegay. [Now chiefly Scotch.]
{{smaller block|Vynes . . . with wondere grete ''bobbis'' of grapes.
{{right|''MS. in Halliwell.''}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The rose an’ hawthorn sweet I’ll twine
To make a ''bob'' for thee. ''Hogg'', The Hay-makers.</poem>}}
'''2†.''' The seed-vessel of flax, hops, etc.—'''3.''' Any small round object swinging or playing loosely at the end of a cord, line, flexible chain, wire, rod, or the like. {{smaller|Specifically—(''a'') A little pendant or ornament so attached; an ear-drop.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>In jewels dressed, and at each ear a ''bob''.</poem>
{{right|''Dryden'', tr. of Juvenal’s Satires, vi.}}}}
{{smaller block|Those Indians who are found to wear all the gold they have in the world in a ''bob'' at the nose.
{{right|''Goldsmith'', Citizen of the World, lii.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') The ball or weight at the end of a pendulum, plumb-line, and the like. (''c'') The movable weight on the graduated arm of a steelyard. (''d'') A knot of worms, rags, or other lures, fixed to a string, with or without a hook, and used in angling. (''e'') Formerly, a grub or larva of a beetle used for bait.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Yellow ''bobs'' turned up before the plough
Are chiefest bait with cork and lead enough.</poem>
{{right|''J. Dennys'', Secrets of Angling, ii. (1613).}}}}
{{smaller|(''f'') A gang of fish-hooks.}}
{{smaller block|The ''bob'' . . . is formed by tying three hooks together, back to back, and covering their shanks with a portion of a deer’s tail; . . . strips of red flannel or red feathers are sometimes added, . . . forming a kind of tassel, with the points of the hooks projecting at equal distances.
{{right|''The Century'', XXVI. 383.}}}}
{{smaller block|(''g'') A float or cork for a fish-line.}}

'''4.''' A small wheel made entirely of a thick piece of bull-neck or sea-cow leather, perforated for the reception of the spindle, used for polishing the inside of the bowls of spoons and the concave portions of other articles.—'''5†.''' The words repeated at the end of a stanza; the burden of a song.
{{smaller block|“To bed, to bed,” will be the ''bob'' of the song.
{{right|''Sir R. L’Estrange'', Fables.}}}}

'''6.''' A short jerking action or motion: as, a ''bob'' of the head.—'''7.''' In change-ringing, a set of changes which may be rung on 6, 8, 10, or 12 bells. {{smaller|That rung on 6 bells is called a ''bob minor''; on 8 bells, a ''bob major''; on 10 bells, a ''bob royal''; and on 12 bells, a ''bob maximus''.}}

'''8.''' A triangular or four-sided frame of iron or wood, vibrating on an axis, by the aid of which the motion of the connecting-rod of an engine is communicated to a pump-rod, the former being usually horizontal, the latter vertical or considerably inclined.—'''9.''' A dance. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|O what’n a ''bob'' was the ''bob'' o’ Dunblane.
{{right|''Jacobite Song.''}}}}

'''10.''' A particular kind of wig; a bob-wig.
{{smaller block|A plain brown ''bob'' he wore.
{{right|''Shenstone'', Extent of Cookery.}}}}
{{smaller block|He had seen flaxen ''bobs'' succeeded by majors, which in their turn gave way to negligents, which were at last totally routed by bags and ramilies.
{{right|''Goldsmith'', Richard Nash.}}}}

'''11.''' A shilling. Formerly ''bobstick''. [Slang.]

{{smaller block|“Well, please yourself,” quoth the tinker; “you shall have the books for four ''bob.''” . . . “Four ''bobs'' — four shillings: it is a great sum,” said Lenny.
{{right|''Bulwer'', My Novel, iv. 5.}}}}
'''12.''' An infantry soldier: as, the light ''bobs:'' possibly so called because soldiers were enlisted in England with a shilling. [Slang.] — '''13.''' A seat mounted on short runners, used either for pleasure coasting or for the conveyance of loads over ice or snow; a sled. [American.] — {{smaller|'''Bob at the bolster.''' Same as ''cushion-dance.'' — '''Dry bob,''' at Eton College, England, a boy who devotes himself to cricket or foot-ball: in opposition to ''wet bob,'' one who makes boating his principal recreation. — '''Oscillating''' or '''rocking bob.''' Same as ''balance-bob.''}}

'''bob<sup>1</sup>''' (bob), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''bobbed'', ppr. ''bobbing.''   [< ''bob''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'', 3, from the vibrating movement; cf. Icel. ''boppa'', wave up and down. In sense I., 2, there is reference to the short, cut-off appearance of bobs. In sense II., 4, < ''bob''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'', 3 (''d'') (''e''). This verb is probably in part vaguely imitative, and not directly connected with the noun.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To cause a short jerky motion of; effect by a short jerking movement: as, “he ''bobbed'' his head,” ''Irving;'' to ''bob'' a courtesy.
{{smaller block|<poem>When Ionian shoals
Of dolphins ''bob'' their noses through the brine.</poem>
{{right|''Keats'', Endymion, i.}}}}
'''2.''' To cut short; dock: often with ''off:'' as, to ''bob'' or ''bob off'' a horse’s tail.

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To act jerkily, or by short quick motions; move or play loosely, in a swaying or vibrating manner: as, to ''bob'' against a person; to ''bob'' up and down, or back and forth, as a pith-ball or other object, or a person. {{smaller block|A birthday jewel ''bobbing'' at their ear. {{right|''Dryden.''}}}}
'''2.''' To make a jerky bow or obeisance.
{{smaller block|He rolled in upon two little turned legs, and having ''bobbed'' gravely to the bar, who ''bobbed'' gravely to him, put his little legs under his table. {{right|''Dickens'', Pickwick, xxxiv.}}}}
'''3.''' To dance. [Scotch.]—'''4.''' To angle or fish with a bob, as for eels, or by giving the hook a jerking motion in the water.
{{smaller block|I’ll ''bob'' for no more eels. {{right|''Shirley'', Hyde Park, v. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>These are the baits they ''bob'' with.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Captain, iii. 4.}}}}

'''bob<sup>2</sup>''' (bob), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''bobbed'', ppr. ''bobbing.''   [< ME. ''bobben'', strike. Origin obscure, perhaps in part imitative; cf. ''bob<sup>3</sup>'', ''v.'' Cf. Sc. ''bob'', a mark or butt.]   '''1.''' To strike; beat.
{{smaller block|<poem>With the bit of his blade he ''bobbit'' him so . . .
He clefe him to the coler.</poem>
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 7316.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I’ll not be ''bob’d'' in th’ nose.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Mons. Thomas, ii. 2.}}}}
'''2.''' To jog; shake; nudge.
{{smaller block|Mr. Harley ''bobbed'' me at every line to take notice of the beauties. {{right|''Swift'', Journal to Stella, Letter 6.}}}}

'''bob<sup>2</sup>†''' (bob), ''n.''   [< ''bob<sup>2</sup>'', ''v.'']   A shake or jog; a blow: as, “pinches, nips, and ''bobs,''” ''Ascham'', The Scholemaster.
{{smaller block|<poem>He that a fool doth very wisely hit
Doth very foolishly, although he smart,
Not to seem senseless of the ''bob''.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, ii. 7.}}}}

'''bob'''<sup>3</sup>† (bob), ''v. t.''; pret. and pp. ''bobbed'', ppr. ''bobbing.''   [< ME. ''bobben'', < OF. ''bober'', mock, deceive, cheat.]   '''1.''' To mock; deride; insult.
{{smaller block|So by siche feynyd myraclis men by gylenhemsilf and dispisen God, as the tormentours that ''bobbiden'' Crist.
{{right|''Rel. Antiq.'', ii. 47.}}}}
'''2.''' To deceive; delude; cheat.
{{smaller block|<poem>Play her pranks and ''bob'' the foole.</poem>
{{right|''Turberville'', A Pretie Epigram.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>You’re ''bobb’d''; ’twas but a deed in trust.</poem>
{{right|''Middleton (and others)'', The Widow, v. 1.}}}}
'''3.''' To gain by fraud or cheating.
{{smaller block|<poem>Gold, and jewels, that I ''bobb’d'' from him.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, v. 1.}}}}

'''bob'''<sup>3</sup> (bob), ''n.''   [< ''bob''<sup>3</sup>, ''v.'' Cf. OF. ''bobe'', mocking, deception.]   A taunt; a jeer or flout; a trick.
{{smaller block|<poem>Let her leave her ''bobs'';
I have had too many of them; and her quillets.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Tamer Tamed.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I am beholding to you
For all your merry tricks you put upon me,
Your ''bobs'', and base accounts.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Wildgoose Chase, iii. 1.}}}}
'''To give the bob to'''†, to make a fool of; impose upon.
{{smaller block|<poem>It can be no other [business]
But to ''give'' me ''the bob''.</poem>
{{right|''Massinger'', Maid of Honour, iv. 5.}}}}

'''bob'''<sup>4</sup> (bob), ''n.''   [< ME. ''bobbe'', an insect mentioned in connection with spiders and lice; = Sw. ''bobba'', a certain insect, buprestis. Perhaps the same word as ''bob''<sup>1</sup>, a bunch, of which a dial. sense is ‘ball’; cf. ''attercop'', a spider, lit. ‘poison-head’ or ‘poison-bunch’; cf. also ''pill-beetle''. Cf. Icel. ''bobbi'', a snail-shell; ''komast ī bobba'', get into a puzzle.]   A louse; any small insect.   ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]

'''bobac, bobak''' (bob′ak), ''n.''   [Pol. ''bobak.'']   The Polish marmot, ''Arctomys bobac.''

'''Bobadil''' (bob′ạ-dil), ''n.''   [The name of a boastful character in Ben Jonson’s “Every Man in his Humour.”]   A blustering braggart.

'''Bobadilian''' (bob-a-dil′ian), ''a.'' Pertaining to or resembling a Bobadil, or a blustering fellow who makes pretenses to prowess.

'''Bobadilism''' (bob′ạ-dil-izm), ''n.''   [< ''Bobadil'' + ''-ism.'']   Blustering conduct or braggadocio.

'''bobak,''' ''n.'' See ''bobac.''

'''bobance†,''' ''n.''   [ME., also ''bobaunce,'' < OF. ''bobance'' (F. ''bombance'') = Pr. ''bobansa,'' ostentation, display, = It. ''bombanza,'' exultation. Cf. ML. ''bombicus,'' proud, ostentatious, < L. ''bombus,'' a buzzing sound: see ''bomb''<sup>2</sup>.]   Boasting.   ''Chaucer.''

'''bobber<sup>1</sup>''' (bob′ėr), ''n.''   [< ''bob''<sup>1</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' One who or that which bobs.—'''2.''' One who fishes with a bob.—'''3.''' One of the artificial flies of an angler’s cast.

'''bobber<sup>2</sup>†,''' ''n.''   [< ''bob''<sup>3</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' One who scoffs.
{{smaller block|Bitter taunters, dry ''bobbers,'' nyppinge gybers, and skorneful mockers of others.
{{right|''Touchstone of Complexions'' (1575).}}}}
'''2.''' A deceiver.

'''bobbery''' (bob′ėr-i), ''n.''; pl. ''bobberies'' (-iz).   [Popularly regarded as a native E. term, < ''bob''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'', ''bob''<sup>2</sup>, ''v.'', + ''-ery'', but really of Anglo-Indian origin, being an accom. of Hind. ''bāp re'', O father! a common exclamation of surprise: ''bāp'', father; ''re'', a vocative particle expressing surprise.]   A squabble; a row; a disturbance: as, to kick up a ''bobbery''. [Colloq. and vulgar.]
{{smaller block|I heard something yesterday of his kicking up a ''bobbery'' in the kitchen.
{{right|''Barham'', Ingoldsby Legends, I. 36.}}}}

'''bobbin''' (bob′in), ''n.''   [Formerly ''bobin''; = D. ''bobijn'' = It. dial. ''bobina'', < F. ''bobine'', a bobbin; of unknown origin, perhaps Celtic; cf. Gael. ''baban'', a tassel, fringe, ''babag'', a cluster, tassel. This would bring ''bobine'' into connection with E. dial. ''bobbin'', a small fagot (unless this is a var. of ''babbin'' = ''bavin''<sup>1</sup>), and ''bobbin'', a little knob hanging by a string attached to a latch. See ''bob''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' A reel or spool for holding thread. {{smaller|Specifically—(''a'') One of the weights used to steady the threads in pillow-lace making, each bobbin having a slender neck around which a part of the thread is wound; formerly made of bone, but now commonly of wood. (''b'') A spool with a head at one or both ends, intended to have thread or yarn wound on it, and used in spinning, in weaving, and in sewing-machines.}}
Hence—'''2.''' Either of the two spool-shaped parts of an electromagnet, consisting of a central core of soft iron wound around with a considerable length of fine insulated copper wire.—'''3.''' A narrow tape or small cord of cotton or linen. —'''4.''' A hank of Russian flax, consisting of 6, 9, or 12 heads, according to the quality.—'''Bobbin and fly-frame.''' {{smaller|(''a'') A machine used in cotton-manufacture for taking the sliver as received from the drawing-frame and converting it into roving or slubbing; this}} is the first or coarse frame. (''b'') A machine which takes the slubbing from the first frame and converts it into a coarse yarn.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
